name: First normal form (1NF)
description: The entry ticket to relational modelling: every column holds a single atomic value, every row is unique, and repeating groups are split into rows. 1NF turns nested or comma-packed data into a shape SQL can actually query.
best_for: Any relational schema — the non-negotiable baseline for OLTP tables
pros: Makes data queryable with plain SQL predicates
Eliminates repeating groups and positional columns
Foundation every further normal form builds on
Trivial to verify and enforce with constraints
cons: Says nothing about redundancy between columns
Naive 1NF splits can explode row counts
Atomicity is judgement-driven (is an address one value or five?)

example.narrative: An order-tracking table packs several items into a single cell, so SQL cannot filter, join or count individual items.
decisions: Row 1001 packs two values into items — a repeating group, which is exactly what 1NF forbids
Each item moves to its own row so every cell holds one atomic value
WHERE item = 'pen' and per-item counts now work with plain SQL

name: Second normal form (2NF)
description: Builds on 1NF by removing partial dependencies: every non-key column must depend on the whole composite key, not just part of it. Attributes that describe only half the key move to their own table.
best_for: Tables with composite keys where attributes describe only one key part
pros: Removes update anomalies tied to partial keys
Shrinks redundant storage of key-fragment attributes
Clarifies which entity an attribute really belongs to
cons: Only meaningful for composite-key tables
More joins than the denormalized original
Still allows transitive dependencies (3NF's job)

example.narrative: With the composite key (order_id, product_id), product_name depends only on product_id — half the key — so it repeats on every order line.
decisions: product_name is stored twice because it depends on product_id alone, not the whole (order_id, product_id) key
Renaming the product would require touching every order line — a classic update anomaly
Extracting products removes the partial dependency; the name now lives in exactly one row

name: Third normal form (3NF)
description: The workhorse of OLTP design: no non-key column may depend on another non-key column. "Every attribute depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key." Most production transactional schemas stop here.
best_for: Write-heavy OLTP systems where update anomalies are expensive
pros: Eliminates most insert/update/delete anomalies
One fact lives in one place — easy consistent updates
Compact storage with minimal redundancy
The industry-default target for transactional schemas
cons: Analytical queries need many joins
Join-heavy reads can be slow at reporting scale
Schema can feel fragmented for app developers

example.narrative: dept_name does not depend on the employee key — it depends on dept_id, which depends on the key. That transitive chain duplicates the department name per employee.
decisions: dept_name depends on dept_id (a non-key column), not on emp_id — a transitive dependency
Renaming the department means updating every employee row; miss one and the data disagrees with itself
After the split every attribute depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key

name: Boyce–Codd normal form (BCNF)
description: A stricter 3NF: every determinant must be a candidate key. BCNF closes the edge cases 3NF misses when a table has multiple overlapping candidate keys.
best_for: Schemas with overlapping composite candidate keys hiding subtle anomalies
pros: Removes anomalies 3NF tolerates in overlapping-key tables
Cleaner dependency structure for constraint enforcement
Forces explicit thinking about all candidate keys
cons: Decomposition can lose the ability to enforce some functional dependencies
Rarely matters outside overlapping-key edge cases
Even more joins than 3NF

example.narrative: Each instructor teaches exactly one course, but the table is keyed by (student, course). instructor determines course, yet instructor is not a candidate key — 3NF allows this, BCNF does not.
decisions: instructor → course is a functional dependency whose determinant (instructor) is not a candidate key — the BCNF violation
The Codd–SQL pairing repeats per student; reassigning Codd to a new course touches many rows
Decomposing on the offending dependency stores each instructor-course fact once

name: Fourth normal form (4NF)
description: Targets multivalued dependencies: when one key maps to two independent sets of values (an employee's skills and languages), 4NF splits them so unrelated facts stop multiplying against each other.
best_for: Tables mixing independent one-to-many facts about the same key
pros: Stops row-count explosion from independent value sets
Each many-to-many relationship gets its own table
Prevents subtle combinatorial insert anomalies
cons: Multivalued dependencies are hard to spot
Yet more tables and joins
Most schemas that reached BCNF are already in 4NF

example.narrative: Skills and languages are independent facts about an employee, but storing them together forces every combination to exist as a row.
decisions: Two skills and two languages explode into four rows — the multivalued dependencies multiply against each other
Adding a third language would require inserting one row per existing skill or the data becomes inconsistent
Each independent one-to-many fact gets its own table: 2 + 2 rows instead of 2 x 2

name: Fifth normal form (5NF)
description: Also called project-join normal form: a table is split until it cannot be decomposed further without losing information, eliminating join dependencies among three or more entities.
best_for: Complex ternary relationships (supplier–part–project style) with independent pairings
pros: Removes the last class of redundancy from join dependencies
Theoretically minimal, anomaly-free structure
Makes three-way relationship rules explicit
cons: Genuinely rare in practice — easy to over-apply
Reconstruction requires multi-way joins
Difficult to explain and maintain in a team

example.narrative: A supplier supplies a part for a project only when three independent pairwise rules all hold. Storing the triple directly hides that the three-way fact is reconstructible from its pairs.
decisions: The join dependency lets the triple be losslessly rebuilt by joining the three pair tables
Keeping the triple table would silently re-derive rows the pairs already imply — redundancy 4NF cannot see
Only decompose when the business rule really is pairwise; otherwise the triple is the fact and 5NF is satisfied as-is

name: Sixth normal form (6NF)
description: Decomposes tables into irreducible key-plus-one-attribute relations, usually with time intervals attached. 6NF underpins temporal databases and Anchor modelling, where every attribute's history is tracked independently.
best_for: Temporal / bitemporal history tracking at attribute-level granularity
pros: Attribute-level change tracking without row duplication
Schema evolves by adding tables, never altering them
Natural fit for bitemporal and audit requirements
Sparse data stores compactly (absent attribute = absent row)
cons: Enormous table counts — queries are join marathons
Impractical without generated views or tooling
Very few engines and teams handle it well
originator: Chris Date, Hugh Darwen & Nikos Lorentzos

example.narrative: Customer name and address change at different times. 6NF gives each attribute its own timestamped relation so histories evolve independently.
decisions: The address changed but the name did not — only the address relation gains a row, nothing is duplicated
A row-level history table would have copied the unchanged name into a new version row
Point-in-time state is reassembled by joining the attribute relations on overlapping validity windows

diagram:
erDiagram
    CUSTOMER ||--o{ CUSTOMER_NAME : has
    CUSTOMER ||--o{ CUSTOMER_ADDRESS : has
    CUSTOMER_NAME {
        string customer_id FK
        string name
        date valid_from
        date valid_to
    }
    CUSTOMER_ADDRESS {
        string customer_id FK
        string address
        date valid_from
        date valid_to
    }

name: Inmon (Corporate Information Factory)
description: Top-down enterprise warehousing: a single, normalized (3NF) enterprise data warehouse is the integrated source of truth, feeding downstream dimensional data marts per department. "Build the warehouse first, the marts second."
best_for: Large enterprises needing one integrated, auditable source of truth across many subject areas
pros: Single integrated version of the truth
Normalized core resists update anomalies and duplication
Subject-area orientation scales across the whole enterprise
Marts can be rebuilt from the core at any time
cons: Long time-to-value — big upfront design investment
Requires strong central data governance
End users still need marts; the EDW itself is analyst-hostile
Heavyweight for small teams or single-domain scopes

example.narrative: Two source systems disagree about the same customer. The EDW integrates them into one normalized subject-area record; marts are projected from it.
decisions: Matching crm 77 to account A-901 happens once, centrally — every downstream mart inherits the same identity decision
The EDW stays 3NF so integration facts are stored exactly once
Departmental marts denormalize from the EDW; they can always be rebuilt from the core

diagram:
flowchart LR
    CRM[CRM] --> STG[Staging]
    BILL[Billing] --> STG
    STG --> EDW[(3NF EDW)]
    EDW --> M1[Finance mart]
    EDW --> M2[Marketing mart]

name: Kimball dimensional modelling
description: Bottom-up warehousing: deliver business-process-aligned star schemas mart by mart, tied together through conformed dimensions on the "bus architecture". Facts hold measurements; dimensions hold context.
best_for: BI-driven teams that need queryable, business-friendly marts delivered incrementally
pros: Fast incremental delivery, one business process at a time
Star schemas are intuitive for analysts and BI tools
Conformed dimensions stitch marts into an enterprise view
Rich, battle-tested technique library (SCDs, bridges, factless facts)
cons: Conformed-dimension discipline erodes without governance
Denormalization trades storage and update cost for read speed
Late-arriving integration needs can force mart rework
Less suited as a system-of-record archive

example.narrative: Delivery starts from one business process — sales — modelled at line-item grain, with dimensions conformed so later marts join the bus.
decisions: Grain declared first: one row per order line — every measure must be true at that grain
dim_product is conformed: the returns mart shipped next quarter reuses it, enabling drill-across
Facts are numeric and additive; descriptive context lives in the dimensions

diagram:
erDiagram
    DIM_DATE ||--o{ FACT_SALES : dates
    DIM_PRODUCT ||--o{ FACT_SALES : describes
    DIM_STORE ||--o{ FACT_SALES : locates
    FACT_SALES {
        int date_key FK
        string product_key FK
        string store_key FK
        int qty
        decimal amount
    }

name: Data Vault 2.0
description: An agility-first raw warehouse layer built from hubs (business keys), links (relationships) and satellites (descriptive history). Loads are insert-only, auditable and massively parallel; dimensional marts are projected on top.
best_for: Volatile multi-source integration with strict audit and re-statement requirements
pros: Insert-only loads parallelize and never lose history
New sources bolt on without refactoring existing structures
Full auditability — every record traces to source and load time
Separates raw integration from business rules
cons: Table count explodes (3+ tables per business concept)
Not directly queryable — a mart layer is mandatory
Steep methodology learning curve and naming discipline
Overkill for stable, single-source warehouses

example.narrative: The customer business key lives in a hub, its describing attributes in a satellite, and its relationship to orders in a link — all insert-only.
decisions: The hub stores only the business key — it never changes, so parallel loads cannot conflict
Alice's move to Bergen is a new satellite row, not an update: full history by construction
A new source system just adds its own satellite; existing structures are untouched

diagram:
erDiagram
    HUB_CUSTOMER ||--o{ SAT_CUSTOMER_DETAILS : describes
    HUB_CUSTOMER ||--o{ LINK_CUSTOMER_ORDER : participates
    HUB_ORDER ||--o{ LINK_CUSTOMER_ORDER : participates
    HUB_ORDER ||--o{ SAT_ORDER_STATUS : describes

name: Anchor modelling
description: A 6NF-based agile modelling technique from the Swedish school: anchors (entities), attributes, ties and knots, all append-only and temporal. Schema changes are strictly additive, so the model evolves without migrations.
best_for: Warehouses with constant schema evolution and attribute-level history needs
pros: Non-destructive schema evolution — only additions, never ALTERs
Built-in bitemporal history per attribute
Generated views hide the 6NF complexity from consumers
Sparse and late-arriving data handled naturally
cons: Very high table counts, view-generation tooling required
Small practitioner community outside northern Europe
Query optimizers struggle without table-elimination support
Hard sell to teams used to star schemas

example.narrative: Each attribute is its own timestamped table hanging off an anchor; schema change means adding a table, never altering one.
decisions: The tier attribute arrived years later as a brand-new table — zero ALTER statements, zero migration risk
Every attribute row is timestamped, giving bitemporal history per attribute
Consumers query generated views that reassemble the 6NF pieces into a flat shape

diagram:
erDiagram
    AN_CUSTOMER ||--o{ AT_CUSTOMER_NAME : has
    AN_CUSTOMER ||--o{ AT_CUSTOMER_TIER : has
    AN_CUSTOMER ||--o{ TIE_CUSTOMER_ORDER : linked

name: Star schema
description: The canonical dimensional shape: a central fact table of measurements surrounded by flat, denormalized dimension tables. One join per dimension, predictable query plans, and a layout every BI tool understands natively.
best_for: BI-facing marts with predictable slice-and-dice query patterns
pros: Simple single-hop joins — fast, predictable aggregations
Intuitive for analysts; BI tools model it automatically
Columnar warehouses optimize heavily for this shape
Well-documented technique catalog (SCDs, role-playing dims)
cons: Dimension denormalization duplicates attribute data
Grain changes force fact-table rebuilds
Weak fit for highly volatile or many-to-many relationships

example.narrative: One fact table of sales measurements joined to flat, denormalized dimensions — every analytical question is one hop away.
decisions: dim_product deliberately repeats Stationery per product — denormalization traded for single-join queries
Sales by category is one join and one GROUP BY; no hierarchy tables to traverse
Surrogate keys insulate the star from source-system key changes

diagram:
erDiagram
    DIM_DATE ||--o{ FACT_SALES : dates
    DIM_PRODUCT ||--o{ FACT_SALES : describes
    DIM_STORE ||--o{ FACT_SALES : locates
    DIM_CUSTOMER ||--o{ FACT_SALES : buys
    FACT_SALES {
        int date_key FK
        string product_key FK
        string store_key FK
        string customer_key FK
        int qty
        decimal amount
    }

name: Snowflake schema
description: A star schema whose dimensions are re-normalized into hierarchies (product → subcategory → category). Trades the star's simplicity for less redundancy and cleaner hierarchy maintenance.
best_for: Deep, frequently-updated dimension hierarchies shared across many facts
pros: Less storage redundancy in large dimensions
Hierarchy levels update in exactly one place
Enforces referential integrity within hierarchies
cons: More joins — slower and harder for ad-hoc analysts
BI tools need extra modelling to hide the sprawl
Modern columnar storage makes the space savings marginal

example.narrative: The product dimension is re-normalized into a hierarchy so each level is stored once and updated in one place.
decisions: Renaming the Stationery category touches one row instead of every product
The price: category-level analysis now needs two extra joins compared to a flat star dimension
Worth it only when hierarchies are deep, large and frequently maintained

diagram:
erDiagram
    DIM_CATEGORY ||--o{ DIM_SUBCATEGORY : groups
    DIM_SUBCATEGORY ||--o{ DIM_PRODUCT : groups
    DIM_PRODUCT ||--o{ FACT_SALES : describes
    FACT_SALES {
        string product_key FK
        int qty
    }

name: Galaxy schema (fact constellation)
description: Multiple fact tables sharing conformed dimensions in one integrated model — effectively several stars overlaid. This is what a mature Kimball bus architecture converges to.
best_for: Cross-process analysis over multiple business events sharing dimensions
pros: Cross-fact analysis through shared conformed dimensions
Avoids duplicating dimensions per mart
Models the real multi-process enterprise honestly
cons: Fact-to-fact queries (drill-across) are easy to get wrong
Conformance discipline required across all teams
Complexity grows quickly with each added fact table

example.narrative: Sales and inventory facts share the date and product dimensions, so cross-process questions drill across the constellation.
decisions: Both facts join the same conformed dim_product, so sell-through rate (sold vs on hand) is a valid drill-across
Facts are never joined to each other directly — each is aggregated to the shared grain first, then combined
Conformance is the contract: if either team forks dim_product, cross-process analysis silently breaks

diagram:
erDiagram
    DIM_DATE ||--o{ FACT_SALES : dates
    DIM_DATE ||--o{ FACT_INVENTORY : dates
    DIM_PRODUCT ||--o{ FACT_SALES : describes
    DIM_PRODUCT ||--o{ FACT_INVENTORY : describes

name: One Big Table (OBT)
description: Pre-join everything into a single wide, denormalized table per analytical subject. With cheap columnar storage and engines that only scan referenced columns, the classic join penalty argument inverts.
best_for: Fast-moving analytics teams on columnar engines where join elimination beats modelling ceremony
pros: Zero joins — simplest possible querying for analysts
Columnar engines scan only the columns touched
Trivial to consume from notebooks and ML pipelines
Great last-mile serving layer on top of modelled data
cons: Massive redundancy; updates rewrite wide rows
Grain confusion causes silent fan-out errors
No reuse — every subject needs its own wide table
History and SCD handling get awkward

example.narrative: The star is pre-joined into one wide table per subject; analysts query it with zero joins and the columnar engine scans only referenced columns.
decisions: Every dimension attribute is flattened in — category repeats per row, and that is fine on cheap columnar storage
The grain is still one order line; documenting it prevents silent fan-out when someone joins this table onward
Rebuilt from modelled upstream tables on schedule — the OBT is a serving layer, not the source of truth

diagram:
flowchart LR
    F[fact_sales] --> OBT[sales_obt wide table]
    D1[dim_product] --> OBT
    D2[dim_store] --> OBT
    D3[dim_customer] --> OBT
    OBT --> BI[BI and notebooks]

name: Activity schema
description: Models everything as a single time-ordered stream of customer activities (entity, activity, timestamp, features). Questions are answered by temporal joins over the stream instead of bespoke fact tables.
best_for: Customer-journey analytics where time-relative questions dominate
pros: One table shape serves nearly all behavioural questions
New activities require no schema change
Temporal relationships (first-ever, last-before) are first-class
Drastically fewer models to maintain than a mart forest
cons: Unfamiliar query style with a real learning curve
Weak fit for non-event, stateful reporting (balances, inventory)
Young ecosystem with limited tooling support

example.narrative: Every customer interaction is one row in a single time-ordered stream; questions are temporal joins over that stream.
decisions: One shape fits all activities — adding a cancelled_subscription activity needs no schema change
First order within 7 days of signup is a temporal join (first placed_order after each signed_up), not a new fact table
Stateful questions like current balance fit poorly — this models behaviour, not ledgers

diagram:
flowchart LR
    S[signed_up] --> P1[placed_order]
    P1 --> P2[placed_order]
    subgraph stream[single customer_stream table]
    S
    P1
    P2
    end

name: Single-table design (DynamoDB)
description: Fold all entities of an application into one NoSQL table, overloading partition and sort keys so every access pattern resolves in a single request. Design starts from the queries, not the entities.
best_for: High-scale key-value workloads with fully known access patterns
pros: Single-digit-millisecond reads at any scale
One request fetches heterogeneous related items
No joins, no cross-table transactions to coordinate
Predictable cost and capacity planning
cons: Access patterns must be known upfront — pivots are painful
Data model is nearly unreadable without documentation
Ad-hoc queries and analytics require exporting elsewhere
Steep learning curve that inverts relational instincts

example.narrative: Customer profile and their orders live in one DynamoDB table as an item collection, so the app's main screen loads with a single query.
decisions: PK groups the customer and their orders into one item collection — Query(PK = CUSTOMER#C1) fetches the whole screen
The SK embeds the order date so begins_with and range conditions cover order-history access patterns
This layout was chosen from the access patterns first; entity thinking came second

flowchart TB
    subgraph P[partition CUSTOMER#C1]
    A[PROFILE]
    B[ORDER#2024-06-01#1001]
    C[ORDER#2024-06-10#1002]
    end
    Q[Query one partition] --> P

name: Document modelling
description: Model aggregates as self-contained JSON documents, choosing per relationship whether to embed (data read together lives together) or reference (shared or unbounded data stays separate).
best_for: Application aggregates read and written as a unit, with evolving fields
pros: Document shape mirrors application objects — low impedance
Flexible schema absorbs field-level evolution
Embedded reads need no joins
Horizontal sharding is natural at the document boundary
cons: Embed-vs-reference mistakes are expensive to reverse
Cross-document consistency is the application's problem
Unbounded embedded arrays degrade into document bloat
Duplicated embedded data drifts without discipline

example.narrative: An order document embeds its line items (always read together) but references the customer (shared and unbounded).
decisions: Line items are embedded: they belong to exactly one order and are always read with it — one round trip
The customer is referenced: many orders share it, and embedding would duplicate data that drifts
The unbounded case (customer's full order list) points from order to customer, never the reverse

diagram:
flowchart LR
    O[Order document] -->|embeds| I[line items array]
    O -->|references customer_id| C[Customer document]

name: Wide-column modelling
description: Query-first design for log-structured stores: each table materializes exactly one query, with partition keys bounding data distribution and clustering keys pre-sorting rows within partitions. Denormalize freely; write the same fact to many tables.
best_for: Write-heavy, time-ordered workloads needing linear horizontal scale
pros: Massive linear write throughput across nodes
Reads hit one partition — latency stays flat at scale
Clustering keys give free in-partition ordering
Tunable consistency per query
cons: One table per query pattern — storage multiplies
Unbounded or hot partitions wreck performance
No joins, minimal aggregations, no ad-hoc queries
Application owns multi-table write consistency

example.narrative: Sensor readings are partitioned by sensor and day, clustered by time descending — the dashboard query reads one partition in sorted order.
decisions: Bucketing the partition key by day bounds partition size — an unbounded sensor partition would eventually hotspot
Clustering by ts desc pre-sorts the latest-readings query; no ORDER BY cost at read time
The region query gets its own table with the same data — write amplification is the accepted price

    R1[23:59 reading]
    R2[23:58 reading]
    end
    subgraph P2[partition S2 2024-06-01]
    R3[23:59 reading]
    end
    Q[query one partition] --> P1

name: Property graph modelling
description: Entities become nodes, relationships become first-class edges, and both carry properties. Traversals replace joins, so query cost follows the neighbourhood you touch rather than total data size.
best_for: Relationship-centric questions: recommendations, fraud rings, lineage, knowledge graphs
pros: Multi-hop traversals stay fast regardless of table size
Relationships are explicit, typed and property-bearing
Schema-flexible — new node and edge types bolt on
Path queries read almost like the business question
cons: Bulk analytical scans underperform columnar engines
Modelling instincts differ sharply from relational
Smaller talent pool and tooling ecosystem
Sharding a highly connected graph is genuinely hard

example.narrative: People and products are nodes; purchases and friendships are typed, property-bearing edges — recommendations are short traversals.
decisions: What did Alice's friends buy is a two-hop traversal from n1 — cost scales with her neighbourhood, not table size
The purchase is an edge with properties, not a join table — relationships are first-class
In SQL the same question is a self-join pile-up that degrades as the tables grow

diagram:
graph LR
    A[Alice] -->|FRIENDS_WITH| B[Bob]
    B -->|BOUGHT qty 2| P[Pen]
    A -.->|recommended| P

name: Entity–attribute–value (EAV)
description: Store data as (entity, attribute, value) triples instead of fixed columns — the schema moves into rows. Standard in clinical systems and product catalogs where attributes vary wildly per record and appear at runtime.
best_for: Thousands of sparse, runtime-defined attributes (catalogs, clinical data, custom fields)
pros: Attributes added at runtime without DDL
Sparse data stores compactly
One physical shape serves unbounded logical schemas
cons: Reconstructing a row means one self-join per attribute
Database-level typing and constraints are lost
Query optimizers handle EAV poorly at scale
Modern JSONB columns cover most of its use cases better

example.narrative: A clinic stores wildly different measurements per patient visit as attribute-value rows instead of a thousand mostly-null columns.
decisions: New measurement types appear at runtime as new attribute values — no DDL, no deploy
Reconstructing a flat row costs one self-join (or pivot) per attribute — the read-side price of the flexibility
Values are stored as strings; typing and range checks moved from the database into application code

diagram:
erDiagram
    VISIT ||--o{ OBSERVATION : records
    OBSERVATION {
        string visit_id FK
        string attribute
        string value
    }

name: Event sourcing
description: Persist every state change as an immutable, append-only event; current state is a fold over the log. Read models are projections rebuilt from events, usually paired with CQRS.
best_for: Domains where the audit trail is the business: ledgers, orders, compliance-heavy systems
pros: Complete, replayable audit history by construction
New read models projected retroactively from day-one data
Append-only writes are fast and conflict-free
Temporal debugging — reconstruct state at any moment
cons: Event schema evolution (versioning, upcasting) is hard
Eventually-consistent projections complicate UX
Querying current state needs materialized projections
Significant architectural buy-in — hard to retrofit or exit

example.narrative: An account's balance is never stored as state — it is the fold of an immutable event log, and read models are projections.
decisions: The balance 70 is computed by folding events 1-3; the log is the source of truth, the projection is disposable
A new monthly-spend report is a fresh projection replayed over events from day one — retroactive by design
Correcting a mistake appends a compensating event; history is never rewritten

flowchart LR
    E1[AccountOpened] --> E2[Deposited 100]
    E2 --> E3[Withdrew 30]
    E3 --> F[fold]
    F --> S[balance 70]
    F --> R[monthly report projection]

name: Time-series modelling
description: Timestamp-first design: measurements keyed by time and tags, stored in time-partitioned chunks with retention, downsampling and continuous aggregation as schema-level concerns.
best_for: Metrics, IoT and telemetry with time-windowed queries and retention policies
pros: Extreme ingest rates via time-ordered appends
Time-bucketed compression shrinks storage dramatically
Window aggregations and gap-filling are first-class
Retention and downsampling automate lifecycle management
cons: High tag cardinality degrades most engines
Poor fit for entity-centric relational questions
Late or out-of-order data needs careful handling
Schema (tags vs fields) is hard to change after ingest

example.narrative: Readings are keyed by time plus low-cardinality tags, stored in time-partitioned chunks with retention and downsampling as policies.
decisions: sensor_id and region are tags (indexed, low cardinality); temperature is a field — swapping these ruins performance
Data lands in time chunks, so retention is dropping whole chunks, not deleting rows
The 1h continuous aggregate serves dashboards; raw rows expire after 30 days

diagram:
flowchart LR
    W[writes] --> C1[chunk June 1]
    W --> C2[chunk June 2]
    C1 --> AGG[1h continuous aggregate]
    C2 --> AGG
    C1 -.retention drop.-> X[expired]

name: Medallion architecture (bronze/silver/gold)
description: Layered lakehouse refinement: bronze lands raw immutable source data, silver cleans, deduplicates and conforms it, gold serves business-level aggregates. Each layer is rebuildable from the one below.
best_for: Lakehouse pipelines needing clear quality tiers and replayable refinement
pros: Clear quality contract per layer
Raw bronze preserves full replay and audit ability
Incremental refinement isolates failures layer by layer
Maps cleanly onto lakehouse table formats and orchestration
cons: Data is stored (and paid for) three times
Layer boundaries blur without governance ('dirty silver')
It's a macro-architecture — you still need a modelling strategy inside gold
Latency accumulates across layer hops

example.narrative: Orders land raw in bronze (duplicates and all), get cleaned and conformed in silver, and are served as business aggregates in gold.
decisions: The duplicate ingestion of order 1001 is kept in bronze (replayable audit) and deduplicated into silver
Silver enforces types and contracts; gold holds the business definition of revenue
Any layer can be rebuilt from the one below — bugs in silver logic are fixed by reprocessing bronze

diagram:
flowchart LR
    SRC[sources] --> B[(bronze raw)]
    B --> S[(silver clean)]
    S --> G[(gold aggregates)]
    G --> BI[BI and ML]

name: SCD Type 0 — retain original
description: The dimension attribute never changes after first load: the original value is the fact worth keeping (birth date, original credit score, acquisition channel). Updates from the source are deliberately ignored.
best_for: Durable attributes whose original value is the analytical point
pros: Zero maintenance — loads can skip the attribute entirely
Historical analyses are perfectly stable
Makes 'as at first contact' semantics explicit
cons: Silently diverges from the operational source
Wrong choice if the business ever asks for current values
Mixing Type 0 and Type 1 attributes in one table needs documentation

example.narrative: Alice's acquisition channel is captured at signup and kept forever, even though the CRM later rewrites it.
decisions: The CRM retagged Alice as paid-search, but attribution reporting needs the original channel — the load ignores the change
Choosing Type 0 is an explicit business decision, not a missing feature

name: SCD Type 1 — overwrite
description: The new value simply replaces the old one in place. The dimension always shows current state and history is discarded — past facts silently re-associate with the new value.
best_for: Corrections and attributes where history has no analytical value
pros: Simplest possible maintenance
No table growth
Ideal for fixing data-entry errors
cons: History is destroyed
Historical reports change retroactively after each update
Aggregates cached before the change disagree with recomputations

example.narrative: Alice moves; her address is overwritten and the old one is gone.
decisions: The UPDATE replaced the value in place — sales Alice made while at 12 Oak St now report under 9 Elm Ave
Acceptable here because the business treats address as current-state only

name: SCD Type 2 — add row
description: Every change inserts a new dimension row with validity dates and a current flag; facts join the surrogate key that was current at transaction time. The workhorse of dimensional history.
best_for: Full change history where facts must associate with the value in effect at the time
pros: Complete, queryable history
Facts stay tied to the version that was true when they occurred
Standard tooling support (dbt snapshots, warehouse merge)
cons: Dimension grows with every change
Queries must filter is_current or a date window
Rapidly changing attributes bloat the table (see mini-dimensions)

example.narrative: Alice's move closes the old row and opens a new one; June sales keep pointing at the Oak St version.
decisions: The change is an INSERT plus closing the old row's valid_to — never an overwrite
A fact dated 2024-05-15 joins K1, so regional reports for May still group under 12 Oak St
is_current = true serves the common current-state query without date logic

name: SCD Type 3 — previous value column
description: The row keeps the current value plus one extra column holding the prior value. History depth is fixed at one step, but both versions are available on every row for easy side-by-side analysis.
best_for: One-off reorganizations where 'before vs after' is the only history needed
pros: Both old and new value on the same row — trivial comparisons
No row growth
Great for sales-territory realignments
cons: Exactly one change deep — the second change destroys real history
Extra column per tracked attribute
Awkward for attributes that change often

example.narrative: A territory realignment keeps the prior region next to the new one so both hierarchies can be reported this year.
decisions: Reports can group by region or previous_region to compare performance across the realignment
When the next realignment happens, North is gone — Type 3 holds one step of history by design

name: SCD Type 4 — history table
description: The dimension keeps only current values while every change is appended to a separate history table. Current-state queries stay small and fast; historical analysis joins the history table when needed.
best_for: Big dimensions where current-state queries dominate but audit history must exist
pros: Main dimension stays compact and fast
Full history preserved separately
History table can live on cheaper storage
cons: Point-in-time fact joins are harder than Type 2
Two tables to keep consistent
Consumers must know which table answers which question

example.narrative: The slim current table serves the app; the move lands as a closed-out row in the history table.
decisions: Dashboards join the two-column current table; only the audit report touches history
The split optimizes for the common query at the cost of a second table to maintain

name: SCD Type 5 — mini-dimension + outrigger
description: Rapidly changing attributes are split into a small Type 1 'mini-dimension' of value combinations; the main dimension carries a current pointer to it as an outrigger, while facts capture the historically correct mini-dimension key.
best_for: High-churn attribute bands (demographics, scores) on very large dimensions
pros: Stops Type 2 row explosion from volatile attributes
Facts keep point-in-time accuracy via the mini-dimension key
Current view available through the outrigger without joining facts
cons: The most moving parts of any SCD technique
Attributes must be banded into finite combinations
ETL must maintain both the pointer and the fact key

example.narrative: Alice's spend band changes monthly; bands live in a 4-row mini-dimension instead of new customer rows.
decisions: Monthly band flips update one pointer instead of inserting customer rows
The January fact carries M1, preserving that Alice was low-spend when it happened

name: SCD Type 6 — hybrid (1+2+3)
description: Type 2 rows for history, plus a Type 1 'current value' column overwritten on every version, plus Type 3 comparison ability — 1+2+3=6. Each historical row knows both its own value and the current one.
best_for: Analyses that constantly switch between historical and current attribute views
pros: Report any fact by either the historical or the current value without extra joins
Full Type 2 history retained
Avoids re-joining the dimension to itself for current-view queries
cons: Every change rewrites the current column on all of that entity's rows
Easy to misquery if analysts pick the wrong column
More ETL logic than any single technique

example.narrative: Both rows carry current_address = 9 Elm Ave, while historical_address stays what it was.
decisions: A May fact joined to K1 can report under 12 Oak St (as it happened) or 9 Elm Ave (as of today) — same join, different column
The move updated current_address on both rows: the Type 1 write inside the Type 2 structure

name: SCD Type 7 — dual keys
description: Facts carry two keys: the version surrogate key (point-in-time view) and a durable natural key joined to a current-only view of the dimension. Both perspectives come from clean joins with no column tricks.
best_for: Warehouses that must serve both as-was and as-is reporting at scale
pros: Clean separation: one join per perspective
Current view is a simple filtered view over the Type 2 table
No mass current-column rewrites like Type 6
cons: Two dimension keys on every fact row
Consumers must understand which key serves which question
Slightly larger facts and more join paths to govern

example.narrative: The fact stores both K1 (version at sale time) and C1 (durable key to the current view).
decisions: Join customer_version_key for as-was reports; join customer_durable_key to the current view for as-is
The current view is just SELECT ... WHERE is_current from the Type 2 table — no extra maintenance

name: Backward compatibility
description: A new schema version can still read data written with the old one, so consumers upgrade first and old data (or lagging producers) keeps working. Achieved by only adding optional fields with defaults and never removing what readers require.
best_for: Consumer-first rollouts and reprocessing historical data with current code
pros: Consumers deploy without coordinating producers
Historical data stays readable forever
Registry-enforceable as an automatic gate
cons: Old fields accrete — cleanup requires a coordinated break
Defaults can mask genuinely missing data
Says nothing about old readers meeting new data

example.narrative: v2 adds an optional currency field with a default, so v2 readers still parse v1 records.
decisions: The v2 reader fills currency = USD when reading the v1 record — nothing breaks
Removing total in v2 would have broken every stored v1 record: not backward compatible
The registry checks this automatically on schema registration

name: Forward compatibility
description: Old readers can process data written with a newer schema, so producers upgrade first. Requires readers that ignore unknown fields and schemas that only remove optional fields.
best_for: Producer-first rollouts where many consumers upgrade on their own schedule
pros: Producers ship without waiting for every consumer
Natural fit for protobuf-style unknown-field tolerance
Enables gradual fleet upgrades
cons: New fields are invisible to old readers until they upgrade
Requires discipline: readers must never reject unknown fields
Harder to reason about than backward compatibility

example.narrative: The producer starts writing a discount field; v1 consumers skip it and keep working.
decisions: The v1 consumer was built to skip unknown fields — the new discount flows past it harmlessly
Renaming total instead would have forward-broken every old consumer at once

name: Full compatibility
description: Backward and forward at once: any reader version handles any data version, in both directions. The change vocabulary shrinks to adding or removing optional fields with defaults — the safest and most restrictive contract.
best_for: Long-retention event streams with many independent producer and consumer teams
pros: Deploy order stops mattering entirely
Years-old data and next year's readers stay interoperable
The strongest automatic guardrail a registry can enforce
cons: Most restrictive change set — some refactors become impossible without a new stream
Optional-with-default everywhere can hide data-quality issues
Requires the discipline of never introducing required fields

example.narrative: Every field after v1 is optional with a default, so v1 and v3 producers and readers interoperate freely.
decisions: The registry set to FULL rejects the required tax_id change at registration time, before anything ships
The cost is expressiveness: required-ness must be enforced downstream, not in the schema

name: Breaking changes — taxonomy
description: The changes that cannot be made in place: renames, type changes, dropping or requiring fields, and semantic shifts that keep the shape but change the meaning. Knowing the taxonomy is how teams route each change to the right migration pattern.
best_for: Classifying proposed schema changes before choosing a rollout strategy
pros: Names the risk so it can be reviewed, not discovered in production
Maps each breaking class to a known remedy (expand-contract, versioning)
Semantic breaks get surfaced — the class type systems cannot catch
cons: Classification is judgement — semantic changes are easy to miss
A taxonomy alone fixes nothing without process behind it
Overcaution can label safe changes as breaking and stall delivery

example.narrative: Four proposed changes to an orders schema, classified before rollout.

tables.name: change review
rows: change total from decimal to string

decisions: The semantic change is the most dangerous: every validator passes while every report goes quietly wrong
Each class routes to a remedy — the taxonomy is the dispatch table for migration patterns

name: Expand–contract (parallel change)
description: Breaking changes made safely in three phases: expand (add the new structure alongside the old), migrate (dual-write, backfill, move readers), contract (remove the old once nothing references it). No step breaks a running consumer.
best_for: Renames and restructures on live schemas with independent consumers
pros: Zero-downtime path for otherwise breaking changes
Each phase is separately deployable and reversible
Works identically for databases, APIs and event schemas
cons: Three deploys where a naive rename is one
Dual-write logic is temporary code that must actually get removed
The contract phase is easily forgotten, leaving zombie columns

example.narrative: Renaming full_name to display_name without breaking readers.
decisions: At no point does a reader query a column that does not exist — the break is dissolved into three safe steps
The backfill runs during expand while old readers still use full_name
Contract only ships after query logs show zero full_name references

name: Additive-only evolution
description: The schema only ever gains optional fields; nothing is renamed, retyped or removed. Old fields are deprecated in docs and eventually ignored, never dropped. Boring, and therefore extremely reliable.
best_for: Widely consumed schemas where any break is unacceptable and cleanup can wait
pros: Compatibility holds in every direction by construction
No migration ceremonies — just deploys
Trivial to enforce in CI (reject any non-additive diff)
cons: Schemas accrete deprecated fields indefinitely
Naming mistakes are permanent (see: address_2_final_v3)
Deprecation without removal still confuses newcomers

example.narrative: A currency field is added with a default; the old iso_currency stays as a deprecated alias forever.
decisions: Every consumer keeps working through the change because nothing they read was touched
The deprecated field costs storage and attention — the accepted price for never breaking anyone

name: Schema versioning
description: Incompatible generations live side by side as explicit versions — v1 and v2 topics, endpoints or table sets — with consumers migrating on their own schedule and the old version retired on a published sunset date.
best_for: Deliberate breaking redesigns that additive evolution cannot express
pros: Full redesign freedom inside the new version
Consumers migrate when ready, not when forced
Clear deprecation and sunset communication points
cons: Producers run and pay for both versions during the overlap
Version sprawl if sunsets are not enforced
Cross-version analytics needs mapping logic

example.narrative: The redesigned order event ships as orders.v2 while v1 keeps flowing until sunset.
decisions: The producer dual-publishes during the overlap window — the cost that buys consumer independence
The sunset date is published with the v2 launch, so v1 cannot linger unowned

name: Data contracts
description: Producer-owned, versioned agreements covering schema, semantics, quality expectations and SLAs — enforced in CI and at runtime so upstream app changes stop silently breaking downstream data. Evolution happens by negotiated contract change, not surprise.
best_for: Organizations where producer app teams keep breaking downstream analytics
pros: Breakage surfaces at the producer's build, not in the consumer's dashboard
Ownership and expectations are explicit and versioned
Contract diffs make schema review a normal code review
cons: Cultural change first, tooling second — producers must accept ownership
Contract maintenance is real ongoing work
Overly strict contracts slow legitimate iteration

example.narrative: The orders contract pins schema and freshness; a proposed field drop fails the producer's CI, not the consumer's dashboard.
decisions: The break is caught in the producer's pipeline while it is still cheap to fix
Semantics and SLAs live next to the schema — the contract covers what a type system cannot

name: Online schema change
description: Alter huge, hot tables without locking: build a shadow copy with the new schema, backfill in throttled batches while capturing ongoing writes, then atomically swap. The gh-ost / pt-online-schema-change playbook.
best_for: Large OLTP tables where a blocking ALTER would mean an outage
pros: No long table locks — the app keeps serving
Throttles and pauses under load
Cutover is atomic and revertible until the final swap
cons: Temporarily doubles the table's storage
Long backfills on very hot tables
Foreign keys and triggers complicate most tools

example.narrative: Adding a NOT NULL column to a 500M-row orders table via a shadow table and cutover.

tables.name: migration timeline
rows: backfill in 10k-row batches + capture live writes

decisions: A plain ALTER would have locked the table for minutes; the shadow-copy path never blocks writes
Live writes during the hours-long backfill are captured and replayed so the shadow never falls behind

name: Lakehouse schema evolution
description: Table formats like Delta, Iceberg and Hudi evolve schemas as metadata operations: add columns on merge, widen types, rename via column IDs — without rewriting data files. Guardrails matter: unchecked auto-merge turns typos into permanent columns.
best_for: Continuously ingested lakehouse tables receiving drifting upstream schemas
pros: Adding or renaming columns is a metadata-only operation
Old data files remain valid — no rewrite storms
Type widening and column-ID renames avoid classic Hive breakage
cons: Auto-merge happily absorbs upstream typos as new columns
Type support differs per format — widening rules need checking
Downstream marts still need their own evolution handling

example.narrative: A new batch arrives with a channel column; mergeSchema admits it and old files simply read it as null.
decisions: The evolution touched table metadata only — the 1001 data file on object storage was never rewritten
Auto-merge is enabled per pipeline, not globally, so a misspelled upstream column cannot silently join the schema

name: Event upcasting
description: In event-sourced systems the log is immutable, so old events are never rewritten — instead versioned upcasters transform each stored event to the current shape as it is read. The chain v1→v2→v3 lets decade-old events replay through today's code.
best_for: Event-sourced systems whose event shapes must evolve over an immutable log
pros: The immutable log stays untouched — audit guarantees hold
Replays work across every historical event version
Each upcaster is a small, testable pure function
cons: Upcaster chains grow with every schema generation
Read-path cost on every replay
Semantic drift is hard to express as a mechanical transform

example.narrative: A v1 event with a single name field is upcast to the v2 first/last shape during replay.
decisions: The stored bytes never change — the upcaster rewrites the event in memory on every read
Today's handlers only know v2; the upcaster chain shields them from every historical shape

name: CSV
description: Comma-separated rows of text: the lowest common denominator of data exchange. No types, no schema, no nesting — and readable by absolutely everything, from spreadsheets to warehouses.
best_for: Interoperable flat-table exchange with humans and legacy tools in the loop
pros: Universally supported by every tool ever made
Human-readable and hand-editable
Streams and splits line by line
Trivial to produce from anything
cons: No types — everything is a string until parsed
No standard for quoting, encoding or embedded delimiters in practice
No nesting or schema
Verbose and slow for analytical scale

example.narrative: The order record as a header line plus one text row.
decisions: total arrives as the text 9.98 — whether it becomes a float, a decimal or a string is the reader's guess
A customer named 'Alice, Inc' would need quoting rules that differ per producer — the classic CSV failure mode
Chosen when the consumer is a human, a spreadsheet, or an unknown tool

name: JSON
description: The web's native object notation: nested, self-describing, human-readable text. The default for APIs and configuration — and a frequent, if inefficient, data-interchange workhorse.
best_for: APIs and payloads where nesting, ubiquity and debuggability beat efficiency
pros: Native to browsers and every language
Self-describing with real nesting
Human-readable for debugging
Schema optional (JSON Schema when needed)
cons: Field names repeated in every record — verbose
No date, decimal or binary types
Parsing cost at analytical volume
Number precision pitfalls (64-bit ints)

example.narrative: The order record as a self-describing object.
decisions: Every record carries its own field names — self-describing, but the names cost more bytes than the values
9.98 is an IEEE double in most parsers; money needs a string convention or a decimal-aware parser
Chosen when humans and heterogeneous clients read the payload directly

name: NDJSON / JSON Lines
description: One JSON object per line: keeps JSON's flexibility while restoring streamability and line-based splitting. The de facto format for logs, event exports and data-pipeline handoffs.
best_for: Streaming and appending JSON records: logs, exports, pipeline handoffs
pros: Appendable and streamable line by line
Splits cleanly for parallel processing
Each line fails or parses independently
Tooling-friendly (grep, head, warehouses load it natively)
cons: Inherits all of JSON's verbosity and typing gaps
No cross-record schema enforcement
A single record cannot span lines (no pretty-printing)

example.narrative: Two orders as two independent lines — appendable forever.
decisions: A plain JSON array would need the whole file parsed at once; one-object-per-line streams and tails
A corrupt line 2 loses one record, not the file
Chosen for event exports and log shipping where producers append continuously

name: XML
description: The enterprise markup veteran: verbose, deeply structured text with mature schema (XSD), namespaces, and transformation tooling (XPath/XSLT). Still the contract language of B2B, finance and government integrations.
best_for: Enterprise/B2B contracts where XSD validation and namespaces are required
pros: Industrial-strength schema validation (XSD)
Namespaces for mixing vocabularies
Mature query/transform stack (XPath, XSLT)
Entrenched standards (SOAP, HL7, ISO 20022)
cons: Extremely verbose — tags often outweigh data
Attribute-vs-element ambiguity complicates mapping
Slow to parse at data-pipeline scale
Developer ergonomics long since lost to JSON

example.narrative: The order record wrapped in named tags.
decisions: The currency lives as an attribute — richer than JSON, at the cost of two ways to model every fact
An XSD can enforce that total is a decimal with two fraction digits — validation JSON only gets via extra tooling
Chosen when the counterparty's integration contract says XSD, which in B2B it often still does

name: YAML
description: Whitespace-structured superset of JSON optimized for human authoring: comments, anchors, multi-line strings. The configuration lingua franca (Kubernetes, CI) — almost never a data-interchange format.
best_for: Human-authored configuration; not a data-exchange format
pros: Most human-writable of the text formats
Comments — the killer feature over JSON
Anchors and references reduce repetition
Superset of JSON (valid JSON is valid YAML)
cons: Whitespace sensitivity breeds subtle bugs
Implicit typing surprises (the Norway problem: no becomes false)
Slow parsing, multiple spec versions
Wrong tool for machine-to-machine data volumes
originator: Clark Evans, Ingy döt Net & Oren Ben-Kiki

example.narrative: The order as YAML — fine for a fixture file, wrong for a pipeline.
decisions: The inline comment is why config lives in YAML and not JSON
If the customer were named NO, YAML 1.1 parsers would read a boolean — implicit typing bites real data
Chosen for files humans edit; data pipelines should hand off NDJSON/Parquet instead

name: Avro
description: Row-oriented binary format built around schema evolution: data is written compactly without field tags, and readers resolve writer schema against reader schema at read time. The default of the Kafka/schema-registry ecosystem.
best_for: Kafka event streams and data lakes needing first-class schema evolution
pros: Best-in-class schema evolution (writer/reader resolution)
Compact: no per-field tags or names in the data
Schema travels with the file or lives in a registry
Dynamic — no code generation required
cons: Needs the writer schema to read anything
Row layout — poor for analytical column scans
JSON schema definitions get unwieldy
Slower than tag-based formats for sparse reads

example.narrative: The schema is declared once; the record on the wire is just values.
decisions: No field names or tags in the payload — the schema supplies them, so a million records pay the naming cost once
A v2 reader with an added default field resolves v1 data automatically — evolution is the design center
Chosen when events outlive code versions: Kafka topics, lake landing zones

name: Protocol Buffers
description: Google's tag-based binary format: fields are numbered in a .proto contract, compiled to native code, and encoded as tag-value pairs. The backbone of gRPC and the strictest widely-used wire contract.
best_for: Service-to-service RPC contracts (gRPC) with strong typing and codegen
pros: Very fast, very compact tag-based encoding
Generated code gives compile-time type safety
Unknown fields skip cleanly — forward-friendly
Massive multi-language ecosystem via gRPC
cons: Codegen build step in every consumer
Field numbers are forever — renumbering breaks the wire
Not self-describing; useless without the .proto
Poor fit for ad-hoc analytics

example.narrative: Fields carry numbers, not names — the wire is tag-value pairs.
decisions: The tag numbers are the contract: renaming customer is free, renumbering it corrupts every stored message
An old reader hitting a new field skips it by tag — forward compatibility built into the encoding
Chosen when both ends are services you compile — the codegen tax buys type safety

snippets.name: order.proto

name: Apache Thrift
description: Facebook's RPC-plus-serialization framework: an IDL, pluggable binary protocols and transport layers, and generated clients/servers. Protobuf's older sibling — still embedded in big-data infrastructure (Hive, HBase).
best_for: Legacy RPC estates and big-data infra that already speaks Thrift
pros: IDL + codegen across many languages
Pluggable protocols (binary, compact) and transports
Full RPC framework included, not just encoding
Entrenched in Hadoop-era infrastructure
cons: Ecosystem momentum lost to gRPC/Protobuf
Fragmented protocol variants complicate interop
Weaker tooling and docs than Protobuf
Same not-self-describing constraints

example.narrative: Same numbered-field idea as Protobuf, with the RPC service in the same IDL.
decisions: The same file can declare service OrderService — Thrift bundles what gRPC splits into proto + service definition
Chosen today mostly by systems that already depend on it (the Hive metastore protocol is Thrift)

snippets.name: order.thrift

name: MessagePack
description: "Binary JSON": the same data model as JSON, encoded compactly with type markers instead of text. Schemaless, self-describing, and a drop-in efficiency upgrade wherever JSON is the bottleneck.
best_for: Drop-in JSON replacement for caches, queues and internal APIs
pros: Same data model as JSON — trivial migration
Self-describing, no schema or codegen
Much smaller and faster than JSON text
Wide language support
cons: Field names still repeated per record (unlike Avro/Protobuf)
No schema means no contract enforcement
Not human-readable
No columnar or analytical story

example.narrative: The order as typed binary markers instead of text.
decisions: 9.98 carries a float64 type marker — the type ambiguity of JSON text is gone, without adopting a schema
Field names still travel with every record: compact JSON, not a contract format
Chosen for hot paths (cache values, queue payloads) where JSON parsing shows up in profiles

name: BSON
description: MongoDB's storage and wire format: JSON's model plus extra types (dates, ObjectId, binary, decimal128) with length prefixes for fast traversal. Designed for in-place scanning and updating, not minimal size.
best_for: MongoDB's native ecosystem; rich types over raw compactness
pros: Real types JSON lacks: dates, decimal128, binary
Length prefixes allow fast field skipping
Traversable and updatable in place
Native to the entire MongoDB toolchain
cons: Often larger than JSON (length prefixes cost bytes)
Little adoption outside MongoDB
Field names still stored per document
Not an analytical format

example.narrative: The order with genuinely typed fields.
decisions: total can be decimal128 — exact money, a type JSON text simply does not have
Length-prefixed fields let the engine jump to placed_at without parsing everything before it
Chosen implicitly by choosing MongoDB; rarely picked as a standalone format

name: Cap'n Proto
description: "Infinitely faster" serialization: the wire format is the in-memory format, so there is no encode/decode step at all — plus a capability-based RPC system with promise pipelining. From Protobuf's original author.
best_for: Latency-critical paths where deserialization itself is the bottleneck
pros: Zero-copy: read fields directly from the buffer
mmap-friendly — random access into huge files
RPC with promise pipelining
Schema evolution via slot layout
cons: Smaller community and tooling than Protobuf
Fixed layout can waste space (padding) without packing
Zero-copy benefits vanish once you transform the data
Fewer language implementations

example.narrative: The buffer on the wire is the struct in memory.
decisions: Reading total is a memory offset lookup — there is no deserialization step to profile
The @N slot numbers play the role of Protobuf tags for evolution
Chosen when profiling shows decode time itself is the cost worth engineering away

name: FlatBuffers
description: Google's zero-copy answer for games and mobile: access serialized data without unpacking, with optional fields via vtables. Trades ergonomics for absolute read-path efficiency on constrained devices.
best_for: Games, mobile and embedded reads of static data without parse cost
pros: Zero-copy reads with tiny memory footprint
vtables make optional fields cheap
Random access into nested data
Strong C++/game-engine ecosystem
cons: Builder API is awkward — construction is inside-out
Mutation effectively means rebuilding
Less compact than Protobuf for sparse data
Niche outside games/embedded

example.narrative: Read fields from the buffer through vtable offsets — no unpack step.
decisions: The vtable indirection is what makes missing optional fields cost nothing
Construction happens bottom-up through a builder — the price paid at write time for free reads
Chosen for asset/config data shipped to millions of devices that only ever read it

snippets.name: order.fbs

name: Parquet
description: The analytical storage standard: columnar layout in row groups with per-column compression, encodings and min/max statistics. Every warehouse, lakehouse and query engine reads it; table formats (Iceberg, Delta) build on it.
best_for: Analytical scans over object storage reading few columns of many rows
pros: Columnar: scan only the columns a query touches
Excellent compression per column (dictionary, RLE)
Predicate pushdown via row-group min/max stats
Universal engine support; foundation of lakehouse formats
cons: Immutable — updates mean rewriting files
Poor fit for single-record lookups and streaming appends
Small-file proliferation hurts performance
Write path costs more than row formats

example.narrative: A million orders stored column-by-column instead of row-by-row.
decisions: SELECT sum(total) reads exactly one column chunk of the file — the other columns are never fetched
WHERE total > 500 skips this whole row group via the max stat before reading any data
Chosen for anything analytical at rest; the answer to 'how should I store data in S3' is usually Parquet

name: ORC
description: Parquet's Hive-native sibling: columnar stripes with indexes, aggressive compression, and ACID support inside the Hive ecosystem. Technically excellent, ecosystem-bound.
best_for: Hive/Trino-centric platforms already standardized on ORC
pros: Often better compression than Parquet
Stripe-level indexes and bloom filters
ACID transaction support within Hive
First-class in Hive/Trino
cons: Ecosystem far narrower than Parquet's
Second-class in Spark/cloud-native tooling
Same immutability constraints as any columnar file
Choosing it outside Hive estates adds friction

example.narrative: Same columnar idea as Parquet, organized into indexed stripes.
decisions: The row-index granularity (every 10k rows) lets ORC skip inside a stripe, finer than Parquet's row-group stats
Chosen mostly by inheritance: platforms built on Hive standardized on ORC and it remains excellent there

name: Apache Arrow
description: The in-memory columnar standard: a language-independent memory layout that engines share without conversion, plus IPC/Flight for shipping it. Not a storage format — the zero-copy interchange layer between systems.
best_for: Zero-copy data interchange between engines, languages and processes
pros: Zero-copy sharing across languages and engines
Vectorized, SIMD-friendly layout
Flight SQL moves data orders faster than ODBC rows
Backbone of pandas 2, DuckDB, Polars interop
cons: Memory-oriented — not a compression-first storage format
Uncompressed footprint larger than Parquet
Ecosystem still consolidating on higher-level APIs

example.narrative: The order batch as shared memory buffers no engine re-parses.
decisions: DuckDB queries the same buffers pandas holds — no serialize/deserialize hop between them
The columnar vectors are what SIMD kernels want; the layout is the optimization
Chosen at the boundaries: engine-to-engine, process-to-process, client-to-server (Flight)

name: Lance
description: A modern columnar format built for ML data: fast random access (unlike Parquet), native vector-embedding columns and indexes, and built-in versioning. The storage layer under LanceDB.
best_for: ML datasets mixing embeddings, blobs and metadata with random access
pros: 100x faster random row access than Parquet
Native vector columns with ANN indexing
Zero-copy versioning for dataset evolution
Arrow-compatible in memory
cons: Young format, small ecosystem
Not a warehouse-interchange standard
Engine support largely limited to the Lance stack

example.narrative: Orders enriched with an embedding column for similarity search.
decisions: Fetching row 421 337 is fast — Parquet would decode a whole row group for that single row
The embedding column is a first-class type with its own index, not a float array convention
Chosen for training/eval datasets where you sample rows and search vectors, not scan aggregates
